title: A Fun Way To Get Students Engaged In Great Discussions ussions/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes an improvisational warm-up game aimed at students who struggle to participate in group discussions because they're self-conscious or unsure what to say. In the "ET" game, small groups pick one student to play an extraterrestrial who speaks only gibberish and pantomime, and another to act as a translator interpreting (or inventing) what the ET means, while remaining group members try to learn about the visitor. He suggests modeling the game with volunteers for younger grades, then "turning students loose" to run with it, with an optional variation that removes the translator entirely so students must communicate through movement and tone alone. Linsin argues the game's playful, low-stakes format helps students overcome shyness, teaches active listening, and reliably increases the energy and quality of group discussions afterward.
points: The "ET" improv game pairs one student as a gibberish-speaking extraterrestrial with a translator, while the group tries to learn about the visitor.
Mixing groups randomly and switching them often, and having students stand rather than sit, increases comfort and animation.
A harder variation removes the translator, forcing communication through movement, expression, and tone alone.
The game is credited with reducing shyness and self-doubt, and reliably increasing the energy and quality of group discussions afterward.
quotes: One of the challenges of group work is getting students to actively participate in discussions.
Mix your students randomly into groups of three or four and be sure to switch them often.
Have each group select one person to pretend to be an extraterrestrial who has just arrived on Earth, and one person to be a translator who speaks the ET’s language.
A variation of the game is to remove the translator. See if they can communicate using only movements, expressions, and body language .
The ET game is an improvisational exercise that has a unique way of drawing students out of their shell.
After just one session of playing the game, you’ll notice an increase in participation.
